content: Dientamoebiasis is a medical condition caused by an infection with Dientamoeba fragilis, a single-celled parasite that primarily infects the lower gastrointestinal tract in humans. This parasite is a significant cause of traveler’s diarrhea, chronic abdominal pain, persistent fatigue, and growth failure in children. Historically, early microbiologists initially believed that Dientamoeba fragilis was not pathogenic. In 1918, researchers observed that six out of seven individuals from whom the organism was isolated were experiencing symptoms of dysentery. However, they concluded that the organism was non-pathogenic because it consumed bacteria in culture but did not engulf red blood cells, unlike Entamoeba histolytica, the most well-known pathogenic amoeba at the time. This early misconception may still contribute to the hesitation among physicians to diagnose infections caused by Dientamoeba fragilis. A study conducted in Sydney, Australia, involving 60 individuals with symptomatic infections, revealed that all participants were infected with the same genotype of Dientamoeba fragilis. This finding highlights the potential for specific genotypes to be associated with symptomatic disease. Epidemiological data indicate that Dientamoeba fragilis is increasingly recognized as a prevalent gastrointestinal infection, particularly in industrialized nations. It is especially common among children and young adults. For example, a Canadian study reported a prevalence of approximately 10% in boys and girls aged 11–15 years, 11.5% in individuals aged 16–20 years, and a significantly lower prevalence of 0.3%–1.9% in individuals over 20 years of age. While anyone can become infected with Dientamoeba fragilis, certain populations are at higher risk. These include individuals with weakened immune systems and those who live in or travel to areas with poor sanitation.
